He imagines the sound of the ocean at that time. The ocean, roaring like one in distress, cried out, “O Lord of sacrifice, protect me, protect me!” He gives [the ocean] a likeness to one in distress: [the ocean was] distinguished by long waves spread out as its arms. The reason for its distress [was this]: its belly was split by the force of His fall, whose body was like a diamond mountain.

Then He saw the earth in Rasā, in Rasātala. Who? “Tri-paru” means one whose three parvans, having the nature of the three pressings, are [His joints]; that is, the form of sacrifice. What was He doing? He was splitting the waters with hooves like sharp-pointed arrows. How? He was splitting them so that He reached the end of the waters, although they had no shore. Of what kind [was the earth]? [It was] the support of all living beings, in which, at the beginning, at the time of dissolution, living beings desired to sleep. He Himself held it toward Himself—“held it in His belly” is the meaning. By this [the commentary] indicates that He lifted it without effort.

“He rose from the vicinity of Rasā and shone beautifully. Even there, in the water, [the demon] came toward Him, raising a club and obstructing [Him], whose prowess was unbearable to withstand. [The Lord was] one whose fierce anger had been kindled by the Sunābha disc. Or, [thinking,] “Why should I tolerate this insult while I am present?” His fierce anger was kindled by Sunābha; the Supreme Lord playfully killed [him] like a lion [kills] an elephant—this is the connection with what follows. “He whose cheeks and snout were marked by the blood of that [demon], just as an elephant king, digging up the earth, becomes red-cheeked and red-snouted from red ochre.”
“Prajñāya” means recognizing. Anuvāka is a Vedic hymn; they praised [Him] with words resembling it.

“O Ajita! “Jitaṁ jitam te” is a repetition expressing excitement. “Yajña-bhāvana” means “He is brought about or worshiped by sacrifices.” “Trayī” means consisting of the three Vedas. “Nililyuḥ” means “they became almost completely merged.” “Because [You assumed this form] for lifting the earth, [obeisances] to You as the boar.”

They praise Him while elaborating His identity as sacrifice, with the four [verses] beginning with “rūpam.” “Chandas” means the Gāyatrī and other meters. By restating the meters and so on that are limbs of sacrifice, [the text] assigns them as limbs of the Lord. The lack of a long vowel in “barhi” is an archaic usage. “Dṛśi” means “in the eye.” “Cātur-hotram” means the fourfold ritual action beginning with the Hotṛ.

“Sruk” means the juhū, on the snout at the front of the mouth. The sruva is at the nostrils. “Iḍā” means a vessel for eating. Camasas and grahas are Soma vessels. “Prāśitra” means the vessel for Brahmā’s portion. “Grasana” means the opening situated within the mouth, because things are swallowed through it. “Chewing” means eating.

“Dīkṣā” means the dīkṣaṇīya iṣṭi. “Anujanma” means manifestation again and again. “Upasadas” means three sacrifices. “Śirodharam” means the neck. “Prāyaṇīya” means the sacrifice after initiation. “Udayanīya” means the concluding sacrifice. Those two are the tusks of Him. “Pravargya” is the Mahāvīra; it is performed before each upasad. “Satya” is fire without oblation. “Āvasathya” is the domestic, or aupāsana, fire. The two form a pair. That is the head—the head of Your sacrifice-form. “Citayas” means the brick arrangements, and “the five breaths” means the five vital airs.

“Prātaḥ-savana” and the others mean the positions or seats, or stages such as childhood and so on. Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra and Āptoryāma—these are distinctions of the seven saṃsthās; [they are] the seven bodily constituents beginning with skin and flesh. “Satrāṇi” means those having the form of aggregates of many sacrifices, such as the Dvādaśāha. Asoma are sacrifices; those with Soma are kratus; You are of that form. “Iṣṭi” means the sacrifice, the performance; He whose bond is that alone.

Having glorified the previously mentioned [Lord] together with His retinue, they bow, saying “namo namaḥ.” [He is] of the form of all mantras and so on, and of the nature of action—the form of general activity. Moreover, purity of being is attained by action joined with renunciation; from that comes devotion; from that, conquest of the self and steadiness of mind; by that, the knowledge that is directly realized. To Him [they offer obeisance], and to the guru who bestows knowledge of this kind.
“O Bhūdhara” means “O lifter of the earth.” “Sa-bhūdharā” means “with mountains.” [The comparison is] to an elephant king emerging from the water. “Datā” means “by the tusk.”

It has been said that the earth held by You shines. Now they say that Your form shines through the earth-disc, beginning with “trayī.” “Atha” means “now,” in another sense. “This form of Yours shines with the earth-disc held by the tusk.” [It shines] with the cloud raised or borne by a peak. “Bhūyasā” means “very great”; “vibhrama” means “beauty” or “sport.”

“For the dwelling place of the world.” “Your wife” means “the mother of the worlds.” Since You are the father, this being so, we who are situated there, together with You, the father, will mentally offer obeisance to this mother—or serve her with obeisance. You have placed the power that bears Your own energy, just as a sacrificer places fire by mantra in the araṇi wood.

They say that this too, extremely difficult, was done by You. “O Lord, who other than You would desire, or resolve, to lift the earth?” is the meaning. In You this is not a wonder, because all wonders are in You. Why? Because You are the one who created this universe, which is exceedingly wonderful—or [You created it] wonderfully.
Displaying wonder, they pray with the two [verses] beginning “vidhunvatā.” The auspicious drops of water tossed up by the tips of the shoulder hairs—by these we were sprinkled and purified.

“He who desires to know the limit of Your activities” is the meaning. The universe is bewildered by the connection of its qualities with You through Your yoga-māyā. Therefore bestow auspiciousness upon the universe. The meaning is: “Please favor me so that, knowing You as possessing inconceivable, endless potency, I may worship You.”
“Upasthīyamāna” means “being praised.” “Touched by His own hooves” shows the imparting of the power of support even in water. “Avitā” means “protector.”
“He went” has “to His own abode” understood. Or, it means “He disappeared.”

[His] activities are māyinī—possessing māyā—and are worthy to be narrated. “Śravayeta” means “he should cause [others] to hear.” The short vowel is an archaic usage. “Uśatīm” means “pleasing.” “He becomes pleased in the heart” means that He is satisfied in His own mind.

Although blessings are easily obtained, they should not be sought; therefore he says, “Enough with those blessings,” with insignificant [things]. Nor should one fear that worship is fruitless; he says that for those who worship without seeing another result besides the worship of Bhagavān, He Himself grants attainment of His own abode. Residing in the heart, He knows causeless devotion.
Therefore who, having somehow drunk [this] among the ancient histories, the accounts of past events, would become disinterested or refrain? No one except a nonhuman, an animal.
In the Fourteenth [chapter], the cause of his slaying is now stated: the arising of Diti’s embryo from Kaśyapa at twilight, through desire.
[We heard] about that very same [Lord] by whom the earth was lifted. “We heard from your mouth.”
“Mṛdha” means “battle.”
The reason for [your] goodness is that you ask about the narration of Hari’s incarnation. It is called so because it loosens or frees one from the noose of death.

He shows that very thing. By that narration Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, was [liberated] by the sage Nārada while still a child. When the airplane was brought to Dhruva by Sunanda and the others, thinking that at that time the abandonment of his body would be expected, even though death was near he did not abandon his body. Rather, placing his foot on the head of Death as on a step, he mounted the airplane and ascended to Viṣṇu’s abode. He will indeed say: “Having gone around and worshiped the foremost celestial seat, after the auspicious rite was completed by the brāhmaṇas, he desired to enter it, bearing a golden form” [Bhāgavata 4.12.29].
He introduces the history in order to state the cause of the battle between the two: “Now.” “The history described by Brahmā, after the gods had asked him, was heard by me.”

To introduce the gods’ question, he first presents the episode of the birth of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu, beginning with “Diti,” up to the end of the chapter. “The son of Marīci” means Kaśyapa. “Hṛc-chaya” means desire; afflicted by that, she desired [a child]. Therefore she desired [her husband] precisely at twilight. “That too” means in the sacrificial hall. There also [he was] “completely absorbed.” “The one whose tongue is fire” means the person, Śrī Viṣṇu, the Lord of all sacrifices.

“Kṛpaṇāṁ bahu-bhāṣiṇīm” [Bhāgavata 3.14.16] he will say. There, by the two [verses] beginning “eṣa mām,” pitiableness is described, and by the four beginning “bhartari,” much speaking is described. “Dunoti” means “he afflicts.” “Vikramya” means “having manifested prowess.” “Rambhā” means “banana tree.”
“Āyuṅktām” means “may he join [it] everywhere; may he do [it] properly.”

For women who have received great honor from their husband, fame spreads through the worlds. [It spreads] through offspring, in the form of a son. She is called “jāyā” because he is born again in her, according to śruti.
“Our father did not ask us separately.” The meaning is: although all thirteen of us have equal feeling toward you, it is improper for you to act with partiality toward us.
[A plea] does not become fruitless indeed when [it is addressed] to a great person such as you.
[Diti is] one whose bewilderment, delusion, is caused by greatly increased lust.
In order to avoid the twilight time, he praises his wife with the five [verses] beginning “eṣa.” “Yataḥ” means “from whom” or “from her.”
“Having taken up all the āśramas.” He himself crosses [the ocean of material existence] while causing even them to cross, with difficulty, through giving food and the like—that is the meaning.

“Half of one’s own body.” Because both have equal eligibility in actions. The words beginning with “yat” are connected with “tāṁ tvām” in the third verse. “Sva-dhura” means the burden of seen and unseen actions. “Vijvara” means free from anxiety.
“Helābhiḥ” means “with play” or “easily.” [The meaning is] “we could conquer.” The idea is that, for one with a wife, the senses generally do not stray here and there.

We are unable to imitate you completely, you who perform many acts of benefit, by reciprocating those benefits and becoming like you. Others who long for qualities, who are fond of qualities, are also unable. Even with a complete lifetime. By the word “vā,” it is stated that they are unable even through other births.
Although imitation of you is impossible. “For progeny” means “for producing a son.” “May they not reproach me.” “Pratipālaya” means “wait.”
Not considering his own criticism, he frightens her and describes Śrī Rudra with the seven [verses] beginning “eṣā.” “This is the time of the terrible,” and it itself has a terrible appearance.
“Bhūta-parṣadbhiḥ” means “by hosts of ghosts.”

If it is said that merely facing him should be avoided, then he replies: In the cremation ground there is a whirlwind, a circular mass of wind; the dust in it makes him smoky-colored, scattered and radiant, whose mass of matted locks is [thus described]. His body is covered with ash, stainless and like gold. “The god sees with three eyes”—the moon, sun and fire—this is connected with the next three verses as well. The sons-in-law of one [father-in-law] are referred to as brothers of one another. Therefore “He is my brother, and your devara” was said out of modesty.

“Even so, should he not forgive everything because of his greatness and because you are his kinsman?” To this she replies: “He has no kinsman or other [relative], because the Lord is equal to all.” She states his power: with the foot by which he cast away from afar, like discarded remnants, the beginningless māyā whose enjoyment he had experienced, we hope to receive that [māyā] as mahā-prasāda, after worshiping him with vows.

He says in two verses that one should not mock him by saying, “He is a ghost because he gives up pleasures that are not forbidden.” His conduct is unimpeachable and free from attachment to sense objects. [The sages] desire to break apart [the mass of ignorance].

“Samīhitam” means the intended meaning, in the form of instruction for the world. “Aviduṣaḥ” means “of one who is ignorant.” Or, it means “of whom there is no other knower”; that is, “of the omniscient one.” He calls the unfortunate ones [ignorant] with “by whom.” “Śva-bhojanam” means “the body, food for dogs.” [They maintain it] with the understanding, “This alone is the self, as the self.”

“Ah, his conduct is inconceivable.” Brahmā and the others preserve the boundaries established by him—their respective spheres of authority. He is the cause [of the universe], and by him this universe was made. Māyā too obeys his command. The conduct of the all-powerful Supreme Lord is inconceivable—this is the meaning.
Even though she had been thus informed by her husband, [she acted] like a vṛṣalī, a prostitute.
“Vikarma” means a forbidden action. “Diṣṭāya” means to the Lord in the form of fate. “He lay with her” indicates sexual intercourse.
“Having touched [the water]” means having bathed. Meditating on the pure effulgence denoted by the word “bharga,” the eternal Brahman, he chanted the Gāyatrī or the praṇava.
“By the fault of the action” means by the defect of the act.
“May he not kill [it]” is the meaning. He states the cause of the fear of killing with “Rudra.” “Aṁhas” means an offense; “I have committed” means “I have done [that offense].”

“Rudra” means he who makes sorrow flow away. “To the fierce one” means to the one who cannot be transgressed. “Mīḍhuṣ” means to the giver of fruits to those with desires; “Śiva” means to the auspicious one for those without desires; in reality, to the one who has laid down punishment; and to the one who holds punishment toward the wicked, the angry one at the time of destruction.
“Bhāma” means the husband of one’s sister, a brother-in-law. He whose mercy is great—even toward a merciless hunter. “The husband of Satī” indicates that he himself knows the nature of women.
“The welfare of her own offspring.” “Lokyām” means welfare worthy of both worlds. “From whom the rule concerning twilight has ceased.”

Those faults arise from the impurity of your mind due to lack of restraint; from the momentary fault in the form of twilight; also from transgressing my command; and from excessive disregard for the gods, the followers of Rudra.
For these four reasons [they will be] two lowest sons, condemned sons born from the womb. “O Caṇḍi” means “O angry one.”
“Of the good beings being killed.”
“Śata-parva-dhṛk” means Indra, the bearer of the thunderbolt.
“Sunābha” means one whose arm is noble with the Sunābha [disc]. Because she had said “for me, among those who are angered,” the anxious Diti prays, “May it not be [by] brāhmaṇas.”
Even the hellish beings likewise do not show favor, and those situated in whatever species of life he enters do not show mercy.

The offense that was committed; through it, sorrow; from that, remorse; through that, reflection—the consideration of what is proper and improper. “In Bhagavān Hari”; “in Bhava, Śrī Rudra.” For these five reasons.
Among the sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu, one will be esteemed by the good. He describes that one with the five and a half [verses] beginning “gāsyanti.” “Samam” means “together,” or “equal” or “similar.”

As gold of inferior color is purified by processes such as burning, so, in order to follow, adopt or attain his character, they will purify themselves by disciplines beginning with freedom from enmity.

“The cause of the universe’s satisfaction is that which has Him as its self.” “Sva-dṛk” means the self, the witness of the self. He is pleased by the undivided vision of one for whom Bhagavān alone is real.

The reason for that is stated with “sa vai.” “Mahātmā” means one whose vision is uninterrupted; “mahānubhāva” means one of great influence; “mahiṣṭha” means exceedingly great, the greatest even among the great. Having installed Vaikuṇṭha Hari in the mind purified and made manifest by mature devotion, he will abandon identification with the body and so on.

He states his being a great devotee with “alampaṭa.” “Śīla-dhara” means one of good nature. [He is] a mine, the birthplace, of qualities beginning with fortitude. [He is] delighted by others’ prosperity; when others are suffering, [he is] distressed. “One whose enemy has never existed.” Just as the moon removes the heat born of summer, so he will be the remover of the world’s sorrow.

He states the absence of limitation in vision with “antar.” [The Lord is] one by whom forms are repeatedly assumed according to the desire of His own devotees. “Śrī” itself is the beautiful woman; He is her ornament. “Draṣṭā” means “he will see.”

Asked by the gods whose splendor was destroyed, [Brahmā] speaks in the Fifteenth [chapter]. The seed or cause of this is the curse of brāhmaṇas and the like upon the two servants of Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha. Having thus stated the introduction to the dialogue of the gods and Brahmā, he now introduces that dialogue, saying: “Prājāpatya” means Kaśyapa; “tejas” means semen, because it destroys the splendor of others—this is an archaic [derivation]. [Diti] was apprehensive because the torment of the gods would be caused by her two sons.

By the radiance of that embryo, the world was deprived of light, the light of the sun and so on having been removed. “Hataujasaḥ” means “whose power was destroyed.” “Dhvānta-vyatikara” means “a mixture or expansion of darkness.”

“Vetta” means “you know”; [or] “what do you consider?” “Because of which we are anxious” means “because of which we are afraid.” “Avyakta” means “unknown.” “Whose path of knowledge is not touched [or limited].”

Praising Brahmā as the Supreme Lord, they pray with the seven [verses] beginning “deva-deva.” “Crest jewel of the lords of the worlds.” “Bhāva-vit” means “you are a knower of intentions.” The meaning is: “You know with what intention Diti’s embryo is growing.”

“Vijñāna” means knowledge and “vīrya” means strength—[He] whose power is such. “To one who has attained this body of Brahmā.” “Who has accepted the differentiation of the guṇas” means “by whom the mode of passion has been accepted.” “For the source of the manifest universe” means “for its cause.” Or, “whose source is not manifest and is not known by any means of knowledge.”

Experiencing suffering at every moment because of desire, they praise the desireless devotees and speak in two verses. “Those who meditate on You with undivided, desireless devotion.” “Ātma-bhāvana” means “He who brings living beings into existence.” “The worlds are threaded in Him”; that is, He is the cause of the animate and inanimate manifestation. The reason is that [the universe] consists of effect and cause, in the form of the existent and the non-existent, but in reality is beyond both. “By whom breath, the senses and the mind have been conquered.” Therefore [they are] accomplished in yoga; and therefore they have obtained Your mercy.

Others, however, are constantly afflicted by action, they say, with “yasya.” “By a rope” means “dependent, controlled by a cord.” Or, “to the chief one” means “to the controller in the form of breath.” Thus the śruti says: “His speech is the rope, and the names are the cords,” and so on.
“Whose actions have disappeared because the division of day and night has ceased through darkness.” “Āpannān” means “us who have fallen into misfortune.”

They state the cause of the calamity. “This embryo” is its qualifier. “Deposited” means “placed”; “Kaśyapa’s ojas” means “semen.” “Making all the directions dark” means “making them filled with darkness.”
Knowing Diti’s misbehavior, he smiled and replied, becoming the subject of the gods’ words—their words of petition.
“Born before you.”
“They went to the world called Vaikuṇṭha.”

He describes that [Vaikuṇṭha] with the twelve [verses] beginning “vasanti.” “Those whose forms are like that of Hari of Vaikuṇṭha.” “The motive is the fruit; ‘without motive’ means that no fruit impels them.” The meaning is “by desireless dharma.” “They worshiped” means “they performed worship.”

“Yatra” means “where.” “Śabda-gocara” means knowable only through Vedānta. “Viraja” means the form of pure goodness; “viṣṭabhya” means holding or supporting. “Vṛṣa” means the form of dharma. “Of his own” means “their own.”

He distinguishes the forest there with the four [verses] beginning “yatra.” “In all the seasons there is śrī,” prosperity through the abundance of flowers and so on; [the trees] are endowed with that.

“Caritāni” means activities; “of the Lord.” The mādhavī creepers are spring creepers, blossoming and endowed with honey. Or, the mādhavīs are fragrant flowers of the spring season, whose spreading nectar is accompanied by bees. Even those whose minds are disturbed by their fragrance sing, while repelling and rejecting the breeze that brings that fragrance. By this, attachment to the bliss of worshiping Bhagavān is shown even among Bhagavān’s associates, despite their unsurpassed enjoyment of sense objects.

“Anyabhṛta” means cuckoos; “dātyūha” means the cātaka bird. [The tumult] stops only briefly, for just a moment. By this, the supreme bliss of even the birds there in hearing Hari’s topics and so on is shown.

“Mandāra” and “Pārijāta” are particular celestial trees. “Kurava” is the tilaka tree. “Utpala” blooms at night. “Ambuja” blooms by day. “Nāga” is nāgakeśara. These are kinds of flowers, fragrant even; when the fragrance of Tulasī, the ornament of Śrī Hari, is honored by Śrī Hari, in that forest they greatly honor the austerity of Tulasī. By this it is said that the residents there appreciate qualities and are not envious. Where such a forest exists—that is the Vaikuṇṭha they entered, according to the connection with the preceding [verse].

He again distinguishes Vaikuṇṭha itself. “Saṅkulam” means pervaded or filled. By what? By the airplanes of devotees, visible by the mere bowing to Hari’s two feet, not obtainable by karma and so on. [The airplanes are] made of vaidūrya, emerald and gold. [There are women] whose hips are broad and whose faces are beautified by smiles, whose self is Kṛṣṇa. They did not generate passion or desire through pride and the like, through joking and the like.

Śrī, Lakṣmī, embodied and bearing a charming form, is seen in that world as if sweeping Hari’s residence, making her lotus feet sound with anklets. By her the fault of fickleness is removed; or [she is seen] with her arm released and extended, free from defect. What sort of residence? One with crystal walls, joined here and there with gold for adornment. The effort of others beginning with Brahmā is for this purpose: “May Śrī grant her favor.” The idea is that, although there is no rajas there at all, she is nevertheless seen in that way, moving a playful lotus, because she is repeatedly reflected in the wall-surfaces edged with gold plates, through humility and devotion.

“O dear! O gods!” In that world Śrī thought in this way. What was she doing? In pools whose banks were made of coral and whose waters were pure, like nectar, in her own forest, Lakṣmī’s forest, accompanied by maidservants, she worshiped Śrī Viṣṇu with Tulasī plants. Seeing her own face reflected in that water, endowed with beautiful locks and an excellent nose, she thought that it had been kissed by Bhagavān. By this it is indicated that even Lakṣmī’s happiness of good fortune comes only through the Lord’s grace.

Again, of what kind was that [place]? Those who hear bad stories do not go to Vaikuṇṭha. What are those [bad stories]? Discourses on subjects other than Hari’s creation and so on—His pastimes—namely, talk of wealth, desire and so on, which cause the mind to go astray. The reason they do not go is this: when heard by unfortunate men, those [stories] throw the listeners into hells without refuge. “Hanta” expresses sorrow. Of what kind are they? [They are stories] by which the essence—the merit—of the listeners is taken away.

By way of context, he laments them. Although they have attained human birth, which even we, Brahmā and the others, desired, they do not worship Hari. What kind of human birth? One in which knowledge of truth together with dharma exists, because it accomplishes both. “Are they not bewildered by the Lord’s extensive māyā?” “Bata” expresses sorrow. If this is the connection, not only do those [who hear bad stories] fail to go, but those who do not worship Bhagavān also fail to go, because they are bewildered by māyā.

Again, of what kind was that [Vaikuṇṭha]? It is above us, and [such persons] go there. Who are they? Hari, the best of the gods, by following whom the restraints and observances are far from them. Or, they have cast aside the yamas and niyamas. In another reading, “dūre ’ham,” the meaning is that they have cast aside ego. Their character, beginning with compassion, is desirable. Moreover, through their attachment to speaking among themselves of the excellent fame of their Lord Hari, their minds become overwhelmed, tears arise, and their bodies become thrilled with horripilation. Or, “above us” is an adjective of those who go: because they are free from ego, they are superior even to us.

Then, after entering that unprecedented Vaikuṇṭha, the sages attained the highest joy. The reasons for its being unprecedented are these: it is presided over by Hari, the teacher of the universe; it is the one object of worship among all worlds; it is divine, beyond the ordinary world; and it is illuminated by the radiance of the variegated airplanes of the foremost devotees. “By the power of yoga-māyā” means having entered through the power of aṣṭāṅga-yoga. In the case of the Supreme Lord, however, yoga-māyā should be understood as the play of the cit-śakti.

In that Vaikuṇṭha there were six enclosures, the gates of the outer walls. Not becoming attached [to those sights], but eager to see Bhagavān, they became absorbed in each successive wondrous sight. They saw two divine doorkeepers. They were of equal age, held maces, and had beautiful attire adorned with the most valuable armlets and so on.

He describes those two themselves. They were adorned with a forest garland hanging down from the neck, in which intoxicated bees were present. [The garland was] placed amid their four dark-blue arms. They bore faces that were somewhat agitated. Their nostrils, the open outlets of breath, were [visible], and from them [came the breath].

“Without caring for or asking these two who were looking on.” “The former six” means the six earlier doors. Just as they entered through those gold-adorned, diamond-made gates, so they entered through the seventh door as well. The reason they did not ask is that they move everywhere unhindered, without being stopped. The reason for their fearlessness is that their own vision was without partiality.

“Vāta-raśanān” means naked, wearing the wind as a belt; although aged, they appeared like five-year-old boys. The word “ca” also includes “by command.” “They prevented [them] from proceeding.” “Such” means [they treated them so], although the sages did not deserve that obstruction. “Ah, even here there is audacity”—thus [they] disregarded their splendor. The two had a disposition contrary to Bhagavān, the Lord who is dear to the brāhmaṇas.

Having attained, through great service to Bhagavān, a high position and living here in Vaikuṇṭha with that qualification—or among those who share Bhagavān’s qualities and see equally—what is this discordant disposition in you two alone? [You have made the rule] that some may enter and some may not. If it is said, “For protecting the Lord, this disposition of the doorkeepers is indeed a virtue,” they reply with “tasmin.” “Kuhakayoḥ” means “of the two deceivers.” “Like oneself” means by one’s own example: “Just as we are deceivers, another deceiver will enter.” The idea is that no one comes here except a devotee of Bhagavān. Nor is there fear or suspicion where the Lord is peaceful and there is no opposition. Therefore you two are merely rogues.

While the gods looked on, the sages, who were being stopped by Hari’s two doorkeepers, spoke the three verses beginning “ko vām.” Śrī Hari is their dearest friend, and they were eager to see Him. When that desire was obstructed, anger, the younger brother of lust, suddenly arose; their eyes became agitated. Although they were most worthy of worship, this is the reason why obstructing them and angering them were improper.

The seed of fear and suspicion is distinction, and he says that this exists for no one here with “na hi.” In Bhagavān, whose abdomen contains the entire universe, the wise do not see a distinction between the self and Him; rather, they see the self contained in the Paramātmā, like the space in a pot within the great space. Just as another king may have fear connected with the cutting open of his abdomen, no such fear exists for Śrī Hari. Why? Because what has been specially produced in you two, who wear the appearance of demigods, is nothing [substantial].

Therefore, in order to do the greatest good for you two servants of this Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, let us consider what is fitting in this offense. They state that very thing: “The existence of inner distinction.” By seeing that, go from this Vaikuṇṭha world to the worlds where, for one who sees inner duality, the three enemies mentioned in the Gītā—lust, anger and greed [Gītā 16.21]—arise. Or, go from Vaikuṇṭha to more sinful worlds.

Having understood their terrible speech, having understood that brahma-daṇḍa, the brāhmaṇa’s curse, and having understood that it cannot be counteracted even by a multitude of weapons, Hari’s two attendants, in extreme fear, grasped the sages’ feet and fell flat like sticks. Of what kind was Hari? [He is] the one who caused those two, who feared such sages, to feel a far greater fear.

They replied to those who were repenting, saying, “Alas, we have offended.” “For the sinful” means that the punishment appropriate for the sinful was indeed given by you, Bhagavans. There is no offense here on your part. Therefore may that punishment be ours. [It is] that which removes even all disregard for the gods, the sin consisting of transgressing the Lord’s command. But our prayer is this: through even a small portion of your repentance, which is caused by compassion, as we go down and down into deluded births, may there be no delusion that obstructs remembrance of Bhagavān; rather, may even delusion lead only toward remembrance.

Thus, immediately understanding the offense of his own servants toward the great sages, He went to the place where they were stopped. “Pleasing to the noble” means charming. “Moving His feet” has this meaning: “Displaying and pacifying their anger born from obstructing the sight of My feet, I will go only on foot, under the pretext of haste.” And, filling even the desireless [sages] with opulences through the company of Śrī, He went to make them forgive.

There, he describes in five [verses] the Lord seen by them. “They saw Him who had come”; the same verb continues through the fifth [verse]. He whose suitable traveling paraphernalia—umbrella, sandals and so on—was quickly brought by His own associates. Of what kind? The Brahman that is the fortune, the fruit to be attained, through their own samādhi became the object of their eyes. The two cāmaras had beauty like swans; moved on both sides by a favorable breeze, they waved. The white umbrella was like the moon, and its pearl tassels were its rays; from them water-drops fell. “Śīkara” means a drop of water.

“Kṛtsna-prasāda-sumukham” means [He had] a face gracious toward all—the doorkeepers and the hosts of sages. “Spṛhaṇīya-dhāma” means the abode of desirable qualities. With the portion of a loving glance, He touched and delighted the heart. If the three worlds are intended, His own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, extending to Satyaloka and situated like the crest jewel of heaven, He made beautiful.

He was clothed in yellow silk upon which His broad hips rested, and He was joined with a forest garland made resonant by bees. Or, “making beautiful” is connected with the preceding [verse]. His forearms were beautiful and bore bracelets. One hand was placed on Garuḍa’s shoulder; with the other He rotated a lotus, a playful lotus. In the reading “vinyasya,” the words beginning with “beautiful” are an adjective of the hand.

His cheeks were worthy of the ornament of makara-shaped earrings that cast away lightning by their own splendor; His face was high-nosed and possessed that [beauty]. He had a jewel-studded crown. A most excellent, mind-stealing necklace was situated in the middle of the mass of His arm-staffs, and it rested on His neck.

What more? The pride of Indirā—“I alone am the treasure-house of all beauty”—had been brought to an end in the Lord’s beauty. This was the thought fashioned by His own devotees; the servants reasoned in their minds in this way. Why? [Because His form was] endowed with abundant beauty. They saw Him revealing a form for me, for Bhava, the Lord, and for you. Seeing Him, they bowed their heads joyfully; yet their eyes were not at all satisfied.

He states that for them the bliss of worship was greater even than the bliss of their own nature. The wind carrying the nectar of Tulasī, mixed with the filaments of His lotus feet, entered through their nostrils and caused an upheaval of intense joy in their minds and horripilation in their bodies, even though they delighted in the bliss of Brahman.

He describes in two [verses] the bewilderment produced by joy. Indeed, His face was the inner part of a dark lotus bud; “dark lotus bud” is an extraordinary comparison. His lower lip was especially beautiful and red, and the smile upon it was like a kunda flower. After looking upward at it, their desires fulfilled, they again looked at His pair of feet, whose support was the red-gem-like nails, with their gaze lowered. Looking again and again in this way, unable to grasp the beauty of all His limbs at once, they finally fixed [those forms] in meditation.

It was the object of meditation for men seeking the goal through the paths of yoga, greatly revered, or approved by many knowers of truth. He manifested a masculine form, endowed with the eight eternal opulences beginning with aṇimā, which are innate and incomparable with those attained by others. They praised Him completely.

You eternally shine in the form of Brahman; that is not astonishing. But now You are directly present in the supremely auspicious, pure-sattva, beautiful form. “Ah, what good fortune is ours!” they said. “O Ananta, although You are present in the hearts of the wicked, You do not manifest there; You are not hidden from us. Today You have attained the very root of our eyes. When our father Brahmā, from whom You arise, taught us Your secret, at that very time You entered the cave of our understanding through the path of our ears.”

An objection is raised: “What our father taught us was a different, invisible self-principle. But I must be another, because I am visible.” “No,” they reply; recognition removes the distinction. “O Bhagavān, we know and recognize You alone as the supreme self-principle. With Your pure-sattva form You create, at every moment, complete love in these devotees. The sages, free from attachment and without the knot of ego, know in their hearts that self-principle through firm devotional practices beginning with hearing, made known through Your compassion.”

In order to pray for devotion for themselves, they describe the devotees’ supreme happiness. They do not value even Your ultimate favor called liberation; how much less would they value another position, such as Indra’s? That [other position] has fear placed in it by the swelling movements of their eyebrows. Who are they? O dear Bhagavān, those who know the rasa of Your stories. Your fame is worthy of being sung, a sacred ford, and purifying.

Now, revealing their own offense, they pray for devotion. “O Bhagavān, previously we had no sins; now all of them have arisen, because we have been cursed in connection with Your devotion. Therefore, let our birth certainly be in hell because of our own sins. ‘Nū’ expresses conjecture. But if our mind delights in Your feet—like a bee, pierced by thorns, nevertheless delights in flowers—may it delight in them without considering obstacles. May our words become beautiful through their connection with the beauty of Your feet, just as Tulasī is beautiful through its connection with Your feet. And if our ear-holes are filled with the multitudes of Your qualities”—by asking for the filling of something small, they pray in the manner of a beggar. The hidden meaning is that, because the ear-hole is space and the multitudes of qualities are formless, it can never be filled; therefore hearing will continue eternally.

They say, “Today we are fulfilled. O Puruhūta, O You of abundant fame, You have manifested this form. ‘Eyes’ means the organs of sight. Although You are difficult to behold and unmanifest to those without self-control, You have appeared to us in this way. To You we offer this obeisance.”

In the sixteenth [chapter], the favor shown to the two attendants even in their demonic state is described. After approving the words spoken by those sages engaged in praising Him, He spoke these words, beginning with “These two,” in eleven [verses].
Because, having disregarded Me and made Me insignificant, you two committed against them an offense as great as possible. Therefore that very punishment is accepted [by Me].

Because the brāhmaṇas are My highest deity, I therefore propitiate you today. If it is asked, “What offense of yours?” He answers with “tad dhi”: whatever disrespect was shown to you by My men, that I consider done by Myself.

Moreover, He says that harm has been done to Me alone: the dishonor that destroys the fame of the master whose names the people utter, just as a disease destroys the skin. Disease here means white leprosy.

The hearing of My pure, nectar-like fame, entering and extending through the world down to the dog-eater, immediately purifies it. Therefore I am “Vaikuṇṭha,” the one whose very auspicious, sacred-ford-like fame has been obtained through you as its causes. I would even cut off a lord of the world who occupied the place of My own arm; what then of someone else? My self-praise, however, is solely for the purpose of exalting the brāhmaṇas.

The sacred dust whose abode is the lotus of the feet [of the brāhmaṇas] is Mine. Therefore it has removed all the impurity of the world. Or, the construction is: the sacred dust from the lotus of the feet is in Me, and all My impurity has been removed. I have acquired this disposition through their service. Because of their service I possess these qualities; therefore Śrī does not leave Me even for the sake of a mere glimpse of her. Others, beginning with Brahmā, observe vows for the sake of obtaining a fraction of her glance. This is connected with the preceding [statement]: “I will cut off your contrary behavior.”

Moreover, the brāhmaṇa is My own foremost mouth; therefore, by disrespecting you, My mouth itself has been disrespected. In a sacrifice, although I eat the sacrificer’s oblations—caru, puroḍāśa and so on—through the mouth of the sacrificial fire, I do not eat in that same way. I eat, morsel by morsel and with relish, payasa and so on mixed with flowing ghee from the mouth of a learned brāhmaṇa who eats, satisfied with Me and having offered the fruits of his actions to Me; that is, who is desireless.
